notes: Audit gap A71. A town business's sales move 0.5 percent for each percent the town's employer pay moves: TOWN_FINANCE_POLICY.business.localDemandElasticity in src/simulation/living-world/town-finances.ts. No source backs the number; it is a hand-set placeholder.
The game reads it as an elasticity of a local-serving business's revenue to the town's total wage bill (and to its job count where pay is not recorded).
question: When a town's total employer payroll rises or falls by one percent, by what percent do the sales of its local-serving businesses (restaurants, retail, personal care, repair) move? Is there a measured elasticity of local nontradable sales or employment to local tradable payroll or employment?

sourcesChecked.source: Moretti, Local Multipliers, American Economic Review Papers and Proceedings 100(2), 2010
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Reports jobs per job (about 1.6 local nontradable jobs per added tradable job), not an elasticity of local sales to local payroll; converting needs each town's nontradable-to-tradable job ratio.

sourcesChecked.source: BEA Regional Input-Output Modeling System (RIMS II) multipliers
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Region-specific output and earnings multipliers sold per region; not read into the repository.

title: How far a town's local sales follow its payroll
usableAnswer: One elasticity (with a range) of local-serving business revenue or employment to local total payroll or tradable employment, from a named study or dataset (Moretti 2010 with the conversion shown, Moretti and Thulin 2013, BEA RIMS II household-spending effects, or QCEW county panels), ideally by industry and by town size, so it can be read as data rather than set by hand.
whyItMatters: This number decides how hard a plant closing or a raise hits the shops in town. At a hand-set one half, every town's main street responds alike; a sourced value lets a player's jobs or wage law show the local knock-on a real town would see.
